content.title: About
content.content: Breakfast meat used as an ingredient in an omelet is a pre‑cooked sausage‑type product, usually made from pork, beef or poultry and seasoned with herbs and spices. It browns quickly and adds a rich flavor, aroma and extra protein to the dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Meat is a common addition to omelets in Europe and North America as a fast way to boost breakfast nutrition.
There are many varieties: smoked, boiled, or herb‑infused sausages.
Traditional American "breakfast sausage" typically contains pork, salt, black pepper, sage and red pepper flakes.
Turkey or chicken versions are available for a leaner alternative to classic pork sausage.
In some cuisines the meat is diced into small cubes so it distributes evenly throughout the omelet.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Breakfast meat provides high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains B1, B2, B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Meat supplies iron and zinc, minerals important for immune health and blood formation.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and fat helps keep you feeling full longer after breakfast.

items.title: Flavor enhancement
items.content: Spices in the sausage stimulate appetite and improve the overall taste of the omelet.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Breakfast meat often contains a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if consumed frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Some varieties are high in saturated fat, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Nitrites are commonly added for preservation; excessive intake is considered potentially harmful.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: A minority of people may experience allergic reactions to certain meats or added ingredients.

items.title: Product quality
items.content: Low‑quality sausage may contain excess fat, filler or be insufficiently cooked.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Dice the meat into small cubes or thin slices and quickly sauté in a pan until lightly browned. Pour beaten eggs over the meat, add any desired vegetables, cheese or herbs, and cook the omelet, stirring gently, until set.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the meat in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Observe the “use‑by” date on the label. For longer storage, wrap tightly in a freezer‑safe bag and freeze for up to 2–3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: The Gyro sandwich is a popular Greek fast‑food consisting of thinly sliced meat (usually pork, chicken or lamb) roasted on a vertical rotisserie, served in a soft pita bread with vegetables, tzatziki sauce and sometimes French fries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional gyro meat is cooked on a vertical grill, allowing the fat to drip away while keeping the meat juicy.
The word “gyro” comes from the Turkish “köre” meaning “roasted”.
Original recipes use lamb, but many countries substitute chicken, pork or turkey.
Tzatziki sauce, commonly served with gyro, is made from yogurt, cucumber, garlic and dill.
Gyro is often served with French fries placed directly inside the pita alongside the meat.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Tzatziki’s yogurt base supplies live cultures that support gut health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and yogurt are sources of B6 and B12, important for nervous system function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Gyro sandwiches contain virtually no added sugars, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Vegetable‑derived fiber
items.content: Tomatoes, onions and cucumbers add dietary fiber and vitamins that aid digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tzatziki and some seasonings can be salty, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Meat fat
items.content: Traditional gyro meat can be fatty; those watching fat intake may opt for leaner cuts.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Tzatziki is yogurt‑based, so individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should choose a dairy‑free alternative.

items.title: Street‑food contamination risk
items.content: When purchased from street vendors, ensure the equipment is clean and the meat is cooked to safe temperatures.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Open the pita, fill it with thinly sliced gyro meat, add sliced tomatoes, onions, cucumbers, and drizzle generously with tzatziki. Optionally include French fries, a drizzle of olive oil, or hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The sandwich is best enjoyed fresh. Leftover cooked meat should be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Pita bread and tzatziki can be kept separately in the fridge for up to 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato, ready-to-heat is a pre‑cooked, portion‑packaged mash made from selected potatoes. It can be quickly heated in a microwave or on the stove, retaining a smooth texture and mild flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mash is made from whole potatoes without artificial colorings.
It is often pasteurized to preserve taste and nutrients.
Packaging is usually microwave‑safe.
Several flavor variants exist: classic, cheese, herb, etc.
Convenient for camping, office meals, and school cafeterias.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which supports normal heart and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Contains vitamin C, an antioxidant that helps strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with many ready‑made sides, this mash has a low fat content.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in potatoes aids digestive health.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Provides quick‑release carbohydrates for energy.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties contain added salt; people monitoring sodium should check the label.

items.title: Allergy to additives
items.content: Certain recipes may include dairy or spices that can trigger allergies.

items.title: Heat handling
items.content: Improper heating can make the mash overly hot and cause burns.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: After opening, store in the refrigerator and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the portion in the microwave (usually 2–3 minutes) or on the stove, stirring to avoid lumps. Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or vegetables. For extra flavor add butter, cheese, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened packages in a cool, dry place. Once opened, refrigerate and use within 3–5 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration appears.

rice-brown-with-carrots-fat-added.title: Brown Rice with Carrots and Added Fat

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice with carrots and added fat is a whole‑grain product that retains the bran and germ of the rice grain, complemented by sweet carrots and a modest amount of vegetable oil that boosts energy value and flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice keeps more nutrients than white rice because the outer layers are intact.
Carrots provide beta‑carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
The added oil helps the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Brown rice is a staple in many Asian and Mediterranean dishes.
When stored properly, the product can stay fresh for up to a year.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: The bran of brown rice supplies soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Brown rice releases glucose slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Beta‑carotene from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene is converted to vitamin A, essential for vision and immune function.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: The vegetable oil adds monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Contains magnesium, phosphorus and iron, supporting muscles, bones and blood formation.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added fat increases the product’s energy density, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Allergy to rice or carrots
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to rice or carrots.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Carrots contain oxalates, which can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the product like regular rice: rinse, add water in a 1:2 ratio, and simmer for 30‑40 minutes. Serve as a side dish, add to salads, soups, or use in Asian‑style recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, refrigerate to prevent oil oxidation.
